```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Using State Measures
 of Student Growth
to Inform Local Practice
 (or, “Organic Isn’t Just for Veggies!”)

 June, 2009</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/02.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Session Learning Objectives
1. Steps to go from data to student-level
 action-item
2. How and where local data fits in
3. How data quality and data use are
 related</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/03.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">The Value of Buy-In in Arizona
1. Process was very organic, from both the top
 down and the bottom up (with a little fertilizer )
2. Year-end state data was only good for the
 beginning of the following year – we are
 creating two types of “check point” that schools
 are excited about
3. Quality means the data answers the questions
 you need, and you trust it – teachers must feel
 this too!</div>
```

::: notes
```{=html}
Damians Q1. What are the steps by which large scale assessment data (i.e., raw numbers) get translated into actions effecting the education of students?
```
:::

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/04.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Our Process Was Very Organic and
 Grass-Roots
1. Good access to data for value-added research
 from previous positive relationships
 • Past relationships/credibility
 • Political alignment
 • Collaboration with authorizer
 • Participation in federal grant</div>
```

::: notes
```{=html}
Used the growth percentile data to create a best practices report <br>
Highlighted how the high-growth schools got where they are<br>
Focused on providing a “road-map” to other schools to follow
```
:::

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/05.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Our Process Was Very Organic and
 Grass-Roots
2. National and local partners focused on
 understanding the “quality” landscape
 • Building Charter School Quality grant, we
 were approached by CO and learned about
 Damian’s work in growth percentiles
 • Led to Arizona State Board for Charter Schools
 to redefine quality
 • Led to state policymakers
 taking notice</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/06.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Our Process Was Very Organic and
 Grass-Roots
3. Used the growth percentile data to create a best
 practices report
 • Highlighted how the high-growth schools got
 where they are
 • Focused on providing a “road-map” to other
 schools to follow</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/07.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Our Process Was Very Organic and
 Grass-Roots
4. During research, vetted growth percentile
 concept with schools and learned the best ways
 to explain it
 • Schools loved it
 • Saw credit for growth, not starting point
 • Started calling to see their own data</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/08.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Our Process Was Very Organic and
 Grass-Roots
5. One finding was about the importance of data-
 driven decision-making
 • “A-ha” moment for us
 • Realized that growth percentiles could take
 assessment from “end of year autopsy” to
 “pre-year and mid-year diagnosis.”</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/09.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Our Process Was Very Organic and
 Grass-Roots
6. Became a key talking point for all of our
 management team
 • Goal was to change the definition of quality
 in the state to “individual student level
 growth” and promote “growth to standard”
 instead of “one year’s growth.”
 • We began to vet these ideas with state
 officials, districts, and our schools.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/10.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Our Process Was Very Organic and
 Grass-Roots
7. Meanwhile, we developed and marketed Best
 Practice workshops
 • Data-driven decision-making
 • Professional Learning Communities
 • Saw the growth percentile idea really appeal
 to them
 • Began to focus on how to develop tools for
 teachers to use it more.
 • Led to….</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/11.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Working on Three Types of “Check Point”
 (that schools are excited about)
1. Beginning of year check on growth based on end-
 of-year AIMS tests
 • Damian’s cool student level graphs
 • Class-room level data for differentiated
 instruction</div>
```

::: notes
```{=html}
Damian’s Q2. With regard to your answer to question 1: How/where do local data (e.g., interim assessments, classroom observations) fit in?
```
:::

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/12.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Working on Three Types of “Check Point”
 (that schools are excited about)
2. Online interim assessment in December
 • Produce mid-point growth percentiles
 • Drive instructional decisions between January
 and AIMS in March</div>
```

::: notes
```{=html}
Damian’s Q2. With regard to your answer to question 1: How/where do local data (e.g., interim assessments, classroom observations) fit in?
```
:::

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/13.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Working on Three Types of “Check Point”
 (that schools are excited about)
3. Online formative assessment tool tied into PLC
 concept
 • Test bank/test building
 • Analysis and reporting
 • Professional development and
 communication
 • Goal is to build teacher comfort and capacity</div>
```

::: notes
```{=html}
Damian’s Q2. With regard to your answer to question 1: How/where do local data (e.g., interim assessments, classroom observations) fit in?
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/14.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Quality means…

1. Data answers the questions you need (i.e. you
 can USE it)
 • Has policy relevance
 • Has classroom relevance
 • Teachers can quickly understand it</div>
```

::: notes
```{=html}
Damians Q3. Thinking of data broadly (large scale, small scale, ...), how are data quality and data use related.
```
:::

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/15.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Quality means…

2. You trust the data
 • Reliable (would get same results again)
 • Valid (measures what you want to measure)
 • Transparent (we can see where the data came
 from and how the results were created)</div>
```

::: notes
```{=html}
Damian’s Q2. With regard to your answer to question 1: How/where do local data (e.g., interim assessments, classroom observations) fit in?
```
:::

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/16.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Final Thoughts

1. Need to treat the whole process like a change
 management issue
2. The state/school feedback loop is critical
3. It’s All about relationships
4. It’s a GREAT time to be in education policy!</div>
```
